content.title: How much will the Artemis II astronauts get paid for their trip around the moon?
content.text: Astronauts, despite the unique job title, are still government employees. In general, they get paid less than you might think. WASHINGTON — A team of four astronauts launched from NASA's Kennedy Space Center on Wednesday and are flying around the moon on a 10-day journey. But they won't be getting overtime for the trip. Despite their unique job title, NASA astronauts are still government employees, and their pay is less than you might think. U.S. astronauts are paid on a "General Services" pay scale, which is how federal officials calculate how much a salaried employee should make. For astronauts, according to NASA, that comes out to approximately $152,258 per year (as of 2024). That means pay is determined by three factors: the rigor of the job, how long they've been employed by the federal government, and their location. All NASA astronauts are technically based out of the Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas. Most of them have been federal employees for at least 10 years, putting them at "Step 7" in the government's seniority ranking. And they're classified as GS-13 employees, some of the highest on the 15-point scale for determining job difficulty. According to FederalPay.org, which tracks government salaries, most astronauts don't actually earn as much as you might expect. Despite being classified as some of the highest-level government employees — astronauts are often military officers and scientists with advanced degrees — they can make less than $100,000 per year. FederalPay.org estimates NASA astronauts are often paid anywhere from $89,693 to $122,336 per year. The Canadian Space Agency, or CSA, has a relatively similar pay scale based on training and expertise: entry level, qualified level, and senior level. The salary scale for Levels I to III varies from $97,100 to $189,600, according to 2023 data. Senior level is designated for astronauts who have successfully completed a space mission. Despite the pay seeming low at first glance, being a NASA astronaut is one of the most coveted jobs in the world. More than 8,000 people applied when NASA last opened the selection process back in 2024. Currently, there are only 48 active U.S. astronauts. NASA has only ever hired 370 people in total since 1959 for the role. The rewards of the job, ranging from prestige and fame to the ability to leave the planet behind for a time, are enough to draw in thousands of applicants for whom money isn't the main factor. Do astronauts get overtime? The question of overtime became a public curiosity when astronauts Butch Willmore and Suni Williams became stuck aboard the International Space Station due to technical failures in the Boeing Starliner capsule that brought them there. The spacecraft had multiple helium leaks and thruster failures during its first crewed flight, prompting NASA to deem a return in the capsule too risky. Willmore and Williams spent 286 days in space, returning on March 18, 2025, after their planned eight-day mission was extended to nine months. But, they didn't receive any extra compensation for the delay in returning home. "When NASA astronauts are aboard the International Space Station, they receive regular, 40-hour....week salaries," NASA told People Magazine at the time. "They do not receive overtime or holiday/weekend pay." However, as government employees traveling for work, they did have their transportation (the rockets that got them to and from the ISS), lodging (aboard the permanently orbiting laboratory in Earth's upper atmosphere) and meals (yum) taken care of. What is Artemis II? Artemis II is the first crewed flight in the series of missions with the goal of returning astronauts to the moon. It will be the first trip to the moon in over 50 years, and NASA announced last week that the agency is setting a broader goal to establish a permanent base on the lunar surface. The world's first lunar visitors orbited the moon on Apollo 8 in 1968. It took NASA just eight years to go from putting its first astronaut in space to putting Apollo 11’s Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the moon in 1969, beating President John Kennedy’s end-of-decade deadline. Artemis has progressed much more slowly, after decades of indecision and flip-flopping between the moon and Mars as the next grand destination. NASA’s new moon rocket, the Space Launch System, or SLS, has soared only once in a test flight without anyone on board more than three years ago. The crew was announced in early April 2023, when the original goal was to launch in 2024. Three NASA astronauts and one Canadian Space Agency astronaut were selected for the mission. The mission has been delayed several times due to conditions and other technical challenges. But if all conditions hold, NASA hopes to finally launch the four astronauts into space Wednesday for the 10-day mission to orbit the moon. It's the first crewed flight test of the Space Launch System deep space rocket and the Orion spacecraft with the overall goal of return to the moon. Who are the Artemis II crew? Reid Wiseman NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman is the commander of the Artemis II mission. Wiseman is a former U.S. Navy captain, who served for 27 years. His career as an astronaut began in 2009, when NASA asked him to be a flight engineer on the International Space Station. According to his NASA bio, the ISS crew completed more than 300 scientific experiments during their 165-day mission in 2014. He also spent roughly 13 hours as lead spacewalker during two trips outside the ISS. Wiseman is the father of two children who he is raising alone after his wife, Carroll, died. He considers his time as an only parent as his "greatest challenge and most rewarding phase of his life," his NASA bio states. Victor J. Glover NASA astronaut Victor J. Glover is the pilot of the Artemis II mission. Glover joined NASA in 2013 while he was a Legislative Fellow in the U.S. Senate and has previously served as the pilot of NASA's SpaceX Crew-1 mission to the ISS in 2018. Glover has also spent time aboard the ISS. He spent 168 days between November 2020 and May 2021 as a flight engineer aboard the lab, where he completed four spacewalks. He and his wife, Dionna Odom, have been married for more than 20 years and have four daughters. Christina Koch NASA astronaut Christina Koch is a mission specialist on the Artemis II mission. Koch joined NASA in 2013 and was a flight engineer for three consecutive Expeditions aboard the ISS. According to NASA, she holds the record for the "longest single spaceflight by a woman with a total of 328 days in space." She also participated in the first all-female spacewalk. Koch is passionate about hard work and challenges, according to her NASA bio, and she has many hobbies that include surfing, rock climbing, running, and travel. Jeremy Hansen CSA astronaut Jeremy Hanson is a mission specialist on the Artemis II mission. This mission will be Hansen's first time in space, but he has participated in a NASA mission before. In 2014, Hansen was a crewmember of NEEMO 19, living and working on the ocean floor in the Aquarius habitat off Key Largo, Florida. The seven-day mission was designed to simulate deep-space exploration, according to the CSA. Hansen and his wife, Catherine, have three children. The Associated Press contributed to this report.
